column3: A small shop wants to let customers place orders online.
The requirements are fairly simple.
Customers should be able to browse products, choose at quantity and and submit an order.
The shop staff need to see those orders and prepare them.
A development team builds the first version.
There's a website for customers, an application running on a server,
and a database running on another server.
The application handles requests from the website.
The database stores the products and orders.
When a customer submits an order, the application checks the details,
saves the order in the database, and sends back a confirmation.
The team tests it.
Customers can browse products.
Orders are saved correctly.
Staff can see them.
They release the application and the shop starts taking orders.
For the first few weeks, everything works well.
Then the shop runs a promotion.
More customers visit at the same time.
Product pages take longer to load, and some customers get errors when they try to place an order.
The application still has the same features.
But under this heavier traffic, it can no longer respond quickly enough.
The team needs to find out why.
They check the application and database.
In this example, the database is keeping up, but the application servers
CPU is staying close to full usage. A test with similar traffic reproduces the slowdown.
That gives the team somewhere to focus. They could give the application server more processing
capacity. Or they could run copies copies of the application on additional servers and share
the request between them. They decide to try a second application server. Now there are two
copies of the application, both using the same database.
But customers still need one address to visit.
Something has to receive incoming requests and distribute them between the application servers.
The team adds a load balancer to do that.
They also check that either application server can handle an incoming request.
If information needed for a customer's next request exists only on the first server,
sending that request to the second one could cause a problem.
After making the necessary changes, they repeat the traffic test.
With this workload response times improve and fewer requests fail.
The team has changed how the application handles demand.
That change also has a cost. There's another application server to pay for,
a load balancer to configure, and more infrastructure to monitor.
For this shop, those costs are acceptable because customers need to place orders during
promotions. A few weeks later, one of the application servers stops working.
The load balancer's health checks detect that the server is no longer responding properly
and stop sending new requests to it. The other server continues handling requests.
Some requests that were already being processed may fail.
And the remaining server still needs enough capacity to handle the traffic.
But losing one application server no longer means losing every running copy of the application.
Then the team considers another question.
What happens if the database becomes unavailable?
Both application servers depend on it. Neither can save orders without it.
Adding application servers hasn't removed that dependency.
The team talks to the shop owner about what an interruption would mean.
How long can the shop stop accepting orders?
If recovery is needed, how much recently saved data could the business afford to lose?
Those answers matter because there are different ways to prepare.
Backups provide a way to restore data, but restoring a database takes time.
Depending on the recovery setup, changes made after the recoverable point may be lost.
A standby database can keep another copy of the data ready and may allow faster recovery.
But it needs a process for taking over. And the guarantees depend on how data is
copied and how that switch happens. The team chooses a setup that fits the shop's needs and
budget. They test recovery to see whether it meets the agreed targets.
At this point, the design includes decisions about both demand and failure.
There's another issue to consider as well. Who can access the orders?
Customers need to see their own orders. Staff need access to the orders they're responsible for
processing. A working order page is only part of that requirement. The application must
check whether the person making a request is allowed to access the requested order.
Hiding a button on the website doesn't enforce that rule.
These access decisions belong in the design from the beginning, alongside the decisions
about servers and storage. Let's pause and look at what the team has been doing.
They've decided which parts the system needs, what each part is responsible for,
how those parts communicate, and where the data is stored. They've considered how much work the
system must handle, what happens when a dependency fails, and how access to data is controlled.
They've also compared the cost and effort of different solutions.
This is system design deciding how the parts of a system will work together to meet its requirements.
The first version had a design too. One application server and one database server.
That arrangement may be enough for a small workload depending on the business's needs.
In our example, the team made changes after problems appeared. In a real project,
we should consider these situations before release. If the shop expects a promotion,
we can estimate the traffic and test whether the application can handle it.
We can also test how the system recovers from a failure, and check whether the recovery time is
acceptable to the business. We won't predict every problem, but these checks help us find
weaknesses early. As usage and requirements change, we can review the design and adjust it.
